bet.text: A simple robot with two degrees of freedom, a lift and one rotating arm, that could still score L4 coral and net algae; a first version was finished by the end of week 4.

demand.text: For a week 1 event the needs were an L4 auto, coral from the station, L4 and L2, clearing algae and a deep climb, which the team thought basically guaranteed one ranking point. Ground coral pickup and scoring algae were only nice to have: the first was too complex for week 1, and the coopertition point looked unlikely.

auto.text: At the championship the robot ran what the team calls a 4.5 coral auto, a few times reaching 4.83: four coral plus a coral and an algae pickup. The team calls it extremely consistent in qualification, but it scored one coral over all playoffs, after camera disconnects and a reef the team thinks had shifted.

cycle.text: The operator selects things like L1 and L4; position on the field and sensors also decide what the robot does. In a super cycle it picks up algae, scores the coral it already holds in one motion, then scores the algae.
Practice cycles fell from about 7 to about 5.7 seconds with the ground intake.

endgame.text: A redesigned climber holds with a servo-engaged ratchet, added because the robot sometimes disengaged while climbing.
A new climber was also needed for weight: the first climber and the ground intake together would have been overweight.

fallback.text: Before its first event the team planned to cycle whichever coral station was not defended. Afterwards it called switching stations more effort than it was worth, because loading the small funnel took a lot of human player skill, and decided to add a ground intake.

gave_up.text: The robot was about 115 lb at its first event and the ground intake added about 16 lb, so that much had to come off elsewhere.
There was no time to make many spare intake parts before Midwest; plates and tubes slowly broke and the intake broke in finals 2.
On the composite carriage the arm chain gradually lost tension; the team suspected creep, then called it less rigid.

changed.text: The first event's robot took coral only from the human player station, which suffered in teleop under defense; a ground intake came before Midwest. The climber was redesigned, and algae gripper compression reduced because algae fell out.
At the championship a borrowed intake roller got four bolts and glue after rollers pulled out of their prints, and it lasted the event; belt tension was raised.

outcome.text: 39-7-0 in official play; ranked 20 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 98.26, Johnson).

functions.name: Ground intake

solves.text: Stop depending on lining up with the human player station under defense

functions.type: ground intake with floating roller and polycarbonate centering

facts.text: A floating roller lets in coral lying perpendicular to the intake
A bottom roller, instead of just a pad, lifts perpendicular coral
A polycarbonate centering piece replaces centering wheels
Two motors: one set of rollers forward and the other backward keeps a coral in the middle, ready for L1
Added weight, about
The centering flaps are springy and the two sides differ, so a horizontal coral has no balance point to get stuck at
In the design each of the two NEOs drives its rollers at 3.3:1
Surgical tubing replaced the paracord and elastic on the floating roller, which broke over time; the team then thought the tension was too high
For the championship the floating plates got slots, because they had jumped out of their hardstops; polycarbonate plates failed and composite ones went back in
A beater bar was added for the championship, for durability and lollipop pickups
For the championship, surgical tubing on the second roller removed the dead zone that holds coral for L1 and made L1 more consistent

cost.text: It broke a lot at Midwest, mostly from sideswipes; raising the intake when unused mostly avoids them but is not always possible

At Midwest bearing retainer prints tore out until bolts with washers held them, belts jumped off small pulley flanges, and the team says the floating roller's hardstop bolt should sit in a slot so the roller is hard to dislodge
At Midwest, the championship and in practice, rollers sometimes pulled out of their prints because the bolt sits 1/4 in from the tube end
The bottom belt walked off in one match; a bent part added against it got the robot stuck on the reef after L1 a few times, so it was removed and belt tension raised
Bearings popped out before Midwest until printed caps were added, and star wheels slid until hex spacers and glue were added
The bottom roller's silicone came loose at Midwest and the loose part was cut off
Tested on algae, it could not pick it up

solves.text: Hold coral through an algae pickup and score it in the same motion

facts.text: Rollers inside the gripper give more traction on the coral, which is upside down while algae is picked up
Offset from the algae gripper
Made of a composite lighter than polycarbonate
Distance between the coral and algae gripper centers in the January design
The first funnel covered 6 in side to side at the station, kept small for a short, light arm beside the lift
January design: printed body with the gears and belt inside, so that coral cannot catch on sharp corners
Version 5 moved the wheels back, cut away the print where coral turns in, and added a front wedge against a 0.8 in dead zone
Version 5 reaches into the coral
In the February code it had no sensor: a current spike after about the first 0.5 s meant a coral, and the motor turned off; current still detected coral at the first event

cost.text: Onyx gears were beaten up by coral and one broke, so they became aluminum; an extended motor sensor wire also broke, so the motor became a NEO Vortex
The team expected to replace its compliant wheels at least once per event
At the first event the robot was vulnerable to defense, especially with its small funnel

functions.name: Algae gripper

solves.text: Keep algae from falling out of the claw, and score it

functions.type: gripper on the other end of the arm

facts.text: A laser sensor detects algae
After the first event the gear ratio was increased, and the top roller was left unpowered to add spin against net bounce-outs
The first compression change went too far, so 3 in wheels became 4 in

cost.text: At the first event algae often fell out or could not be scored, so compression was reduced
Before Midwest it still had trouble when algae came in off-center

facts.text: Two Vortex motors, an aluminum barrel and Spectra rigging
Two stages instead of the three in the block CAD
Geared 5:1 to a 2 in drum
A wide drum synchronizes the motors and winds 10 ft of rigging, with up and down lines on separate areas; the line wrapped freely, sometimes over itself, and the lift still worked
Oversized pulleys keep the line from skipping out if it goes slack
An extension spring of about 150 lbf/in sets the line tension

cost.text: In first tests it wobbled and the carriage popped out twice; welded steel stays, a stronger crossbar and hard stops were added

solves.text: Stop the robot disengaging from the climb

facts.text: A servo engages a ratchet so the climb holds
Lighter composite parts; weight was cut from the first event's climber
First version: a chain-driven pivot based on the Everybot climb, raised to clear the battery and without a winch to avoid the arm
First version weight, about
Midwest version weight, just under
First version: wide wings guide the cage, because lining up was too hard
During the first event a part was sawn off so the hook latched faster, and two bolts stopped the cage rotating out
Midwest version: line behind a 1 x 1 in tube keeps it from bending, and a single-bar grabber is lighter and easier to align

cost.text: Past 90 degrees the composite goes from tension to compression and buckles, so much of it was reinforced or replaced with aluminum for Midwest

functions.name: Covered belly pan

solves.text: Protect the electronics from loose coral

functions.type: electronics on the underside with a polycarbonate piece added

facts.text: If a coral gets stuck on top, lifting the arm a little frees it

solves.text: Always see a tag while scoring on either branch

facts.text: Crossing the cameras keeps a tag in view when scoring the left or right branch
Accuracy at the reef when stationary, with vision, around +/-
When both cameras give an estimate, the robot takes the more trusted one instead of blending them
In autos at the first event it used vision only near the reef, because an estimate from a far tag was a problem
The 12 scoring poses at each reef are recorded with the robot in place during field calibration

cost.text: Crossing the cameras reduces the total field of view

solves.text: Find coral on the floor for a planned four to five piece ground-intake auto

facts.text: Gives a field position for a coral, which the robot drives to in auto
Can switch to tags when not intaking, for three tag cameras
Limelight 3 with a Coral accelerator and the default detection models

cost.text: A coral hit made it disconnect in practice, until another camera was borrowed; a bad power path did so again in early championship playoffs

functions.name: Arm

solves.text: Score L4 coral and algae while leaving space for a deep climb

functions.type: chain-driven dead-axle arm with a gripper at each end

facts.text: Turns on a fixed 1.5 in aluminum tube with large bearings; the arm wires run through the tube
First version: printed shoulder with a 0.09 in plate; arms of stacked 1.5 x 1.5 in tube, because no 1.5 x 3 in tube was found with a 1/16 in wall
Carbon fiber was looked at for the arms and was much harder to make for little benefit
One NEO at about 130:1
A chain tensioner was added for the championship
Balanced, so very low current limits control it and it is fairly easy to push back by hand while holding; in February the team expected that to absorb hits
Near the reef it waits at an angle that clears the reef until the lift is at height; on the way back the lift waits for the arm

cost.text: The center of gravity is high when extended, so the robot waits to extend until it has started aligning
Torque from the arm racked the carriage in practice, so the team decided to double its bearings
During Midwest a forum reader called waiting to extend until fully aligned the huge bottleneck of the cycle
The team answered that consistency came first at Midwest and extending sooner was high on its list for the championship

functions.name: Automated driver controls

solves.text: Keep the driver from remembering many buttons or timing actions with the operator

functions.type: one score button, with robot-chosen side and target

facts.text: In the January plan the operator chooses what the driver's buttons will do; only the climb acts directly
In the February code the robot turns its closer side to the station, net or processor, and picks the station from field position
In the same code one button scores at the reef if the robot holds coral, and otherwise at the barge or processor if it holds algae

functions.name: Maximum-size frame and weight cuts

solves.text: Keep a high center of gravity from limiting acceleration
Make weight for a ground intake

functions.type: largest frame with small swerve modules, lightened for the ground intake

facts.text: Computed acceleration limit before tipping, 30 in wide with the center of gravity 14 in up: 9.1 m/s^2 with its MAXSwerve modules against 8.5 with SDS modules, whose wheels sit further in
After the first event the team reported no problems with tipping, mostly thanks to its maximum-size drive base
Planned savings: arm and carriage 6 lb, climb 6 lb, drive tubes with 1/16 in wall 3 lb, lift 1.5 lb, camera mounts 0.5 lb
All frame rails became 1/16 in wall; the team planned to move parts of the drive base into the bumpers to use spare bumper weight

decisions.choice: Add a ground intake between events
decisions.because: teleop under defense suffered, and other teams were doing well with ground intakes
decisions.instead_of: loading only from the human player station

decisions.because: no wheels are needed after the intake

decisions.choice: Make the carriage, coral gripper and climber from a lighter composite
decisions.because: the ground intake's weight had to come off elsewhere
the robot can pick up algae and score coral in one fluid motion
decisions.instead_of: picking up the algae, backing away and moving the arm

decisions.because: a tag is always in view on the left or right branch

decisions.choice: Raise belt tension on the bottom roller
decisions.because: a bent guard got the robot stuck on the reef after L1
decisions.instead_of: a bent guard against belt walking

decisions.choice: Use one rotating arm on a lift
decisions.because: it could do everything but ground coral and packed a climb a little better
decisions.instead_of: an arm that could not climb within the 18 in extension limit, a chute and lift with a hard deep climb, and a single-stage lift awkward at L2

decisions.choice: Drop passing coral through the arm
decisions.because: the arm moves quickly anyway, passthrough adds complexity, and slow-motion tests did not show instant control

decisions.choice: Use a ground intake that hands straight to the gripper
decisions.instead_of: a 1778-style intake, which needed a complete arm redesign and left climb packaging issues

decisions.choice: Put the intake's leading roller on a pivot
decisions.because: a coral taken in horizontally would otherwise have to go through the hex shaft
decisions.instead_of: raising the intake slightly, which can get fairly complex in software

decisions.choice: Make the intake narrower than full width
decisions.because: it saves weight, and wheels pressed on the tube would spoil the start position used as zero

decisions.choice: Sense algae with a laser sensor
decisions.because: it is a bit more reliable
